name: Eisel-Lemire fast float parsing (fastfloat/fast_float) -- Lemire 2021 peer-reviewed benchmark
workload: Parsing 64-bit floating-point numbers from decimal ASCII strings, single-threaded, across three datasets: canada (111k real-world coordinate floats from a standard JSON parsing benchmark corpus), uniform (100k random floats in [0,1]), and integer (100k random 32-bit integers formatted as text).
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (Daniel Lemire, "Number Parsing at a Gigabyte per Second", Software: Practice and Experience, 2021; arXiv:2101.11408). Table 9, AMD EPYC 7262 Zen2, GCC 10.2 -O3: this-paper's parser reaches 51-70 million numbers/s vs strtod's 9.3-24 million/s (~3-5x) and vs abseil's from_chars 21-30 million/s (~2x); text states "our approach is generally twice as fast as the abseil library and up to five times faster than the standard library." Table 13, Intel i7-7700K@4.2GHz, MSVC 19.26.28806 (VS2019): parser reaches 37-60 million numbers/s vs Microsoft's std::from_chars 6.7-22 million/s (~2.7-6.7x) and vs strtod 6.0-15 million/s (~4-8.3x). Apple M1, clang 12.0.0 -O3: parser reaches 1.5 GiB/s on the uniform dataset; text states strtod is "several times slower than any other number parser" on that platform. Big-integer test on AMD Zen2: parser exceeds 1100 MiB/s vs strtod's 110 MiB/s (~10x) and abseil's 910 MiB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Linux (4 CPU architectures): GCC 10.2, flags -O3 -DNDEBUG. Windows: Microsoft C++ compiler 19.26.28806 (Visual Studio 2019), flags /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG. macOS/Apple M1: Apple clang 12.0.0, flags -O3 -DNDEBUG.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.7GHz); AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen2, 3.39GHz); Ampere ARM Skylark (aarch64, 3.2GHz); IBM POWER9 (ppc64le, 3.77GHz); Intel Core i7-7700K (4.2GHz, Windows run); Apple M1 (ARM, 3.2GHz) -- all named explicitly in the paper's Table 8/13.
stars_or_usage: 2,114 stars; algorithm adopted by GCC 12's runtime, Rust 1.55+, Go 1.16's strconv, Apache Arrow, Yandex ClickHouse (per paper's abstract/footnotes)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11-compliant, no heap allocation; only handles the common case (significand of <=19 digits) directly, needs a documented fallback for pathological many-digit inputs (a 2022 follow-up paper, arXiv:2212.06644, proves that fallback path is in fact unreachable); same Eisel-Lemire algorithm also shipped as lemire/fast_double_parser (also on the exclusion list) and ported to Rust/C#/Java per the paper's footnotes.
caveats: This is a Tier-A peer-reviewed/published benchmark (public benchmark repo https://github.com/lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark tag v0.1.0, plus compiler, flags and CPU model all stated for every platform) for a project already on the exclusion list, reported per the KNOWN_LIST exception for Tier A/B academic evidence; repo_url points at fastfloat/fast_float, the implementation the paper itself cites (footnote 7) as its open-source library.
found_via: arXiv API (WebFetch on http://export.arxiv.org/api/query with ti:/abs: phrase queries after WebSearch budget was exhausted) -> arXiv:2101.11408 "Number Parsing at a Gigabyte per Second" (Lemire, 2021); PDF downloaded and read directly for Tables 8/9/13 and compiler/flag/hardware details.
